name: Gather
tagline: Build a small spatial web room with basic movement and text presence

pricing.basis: annual billing, per user per month

tiers.name: Essential
tiers.limits: Unlimited meetings and chat; recording, transcription and guest hosting included subject to plan usage limits
tiers.notes: Displayed as $12/member/month billed yearly; annual plan saves 20%. The exact month-to-month rate was not exposed on the accessible page.

pricing.freeTierCaps: no permanent free tier; 30-day trial with no credit card, for up to 50 teammates
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual (-20% annually); exact monthly rate not publicly exposed
pricing.hiddenCosts: Charged per registered member, while guests are free. Recording, transcription and guest-hosting allowances are metered, but the accessible pricing page did not expose all exact thresholds.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Gather, build a small spatial web room with basic movement and text presence. The hard boundary is real-time spatial media, maps, integrations, moderation, and hosted capacity, plus network, moderation, and communication infrastructure.
coreLoopDIY: Host a small private spatial web room with basic movement and text presence, organize discussion into channels or topics, and keep membership and moderation under the owner's control.
whatYouLose: real-time spatial media, maps, integrations, moderation, and hosted capacity
ongoingBurden: realtime delivery, notifications, abuse handling, search, media, permissions, mobile clients, backups, and community operations
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Gather because community software is valuable when members are already there and the operator does not have to own realtime reliability and abuse response. The recurring cost buys realtime delivery, notifications, abuse handling, search, media, permissions, mobile clients, backups, and community operations, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Discourse
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source community discussion platform with strong moderation and search.

alternatives.name: Cosmos Free
alternatives.desc: A persistent spatial office for four people with no call timer; the fifth person remains outdoors.

facts.install: Hosted signup in the browser, with optional native desktop and mobile apps
facts.engines: Built-in transcription and AI meeting summaries; the provider and model are not disclosed in public first-party documentation
facts.dataFormat: Account, messages and files live in Cosmos's cloud; calls are transmitted encrypted, while user-started recordings are stored on Cosmos servers and some recording or message data is handled by US processors
facts.gapVsPaid: The four-person concurrent cap and shallow map and game-world tooling make it a much smaller social space than Gather.

alternatives.name: flat.social Free
alternatives.desc: Five people, unlimited sessions and custom rooms; small, simple and refreshingly uninterested in seat arithmetic.

facts.install: Hosted browser signup; guests join by link
facts.dataFormat: Accounts, room definitions and shared content live in flat.social's hosted service; device and usage data is collected by the service, while live media is handled in the browser
facts.gapVsPaid: The hard five-person cap and modest object and room ecosystem are much less capable than Gather's map-building and community features.

alternatives.name: Kumospace Free
alternatives.desc: Five registered members get customizable spatial rooms and basic chat; the sixth seat costs money.

facts.install: Hosted signup in a browser; desktop and mobile apps are optional
facts.dataFormat: Rooms, chat and files live in Kumospace's cloud; audio and video is relayed through Daily or Agora and is not persistently recorded by Kumospace
facts.gapVsPaid: Its five-member, one-floor free plan is less game-like and less extensible than Gather's world-building ecosystem.

alternatives.name: SpatialChat Free
alternatives.desc: Twelve people and four rooms for two hours a day; the office closes itself at lunch.

facts.install: Hosted browser signup; guests join by link
facts.dataFormat: Spaces, uploaded files and account data live in SpatialChat's hosted service; calls occur in the browser
facts.gapVsPaid: Its two-hour daily limit makes it unsuitable as the persistent room that Gather users leave open.

alternatives.name: WorkAdventure Free
alternatives.desc: A pixel office for ten simultaneous people; the eleventh gets bounced.

facts.install: Create a hosted space in the browser, or self-host with Docker Compose or the Helm and Kubernetes stack
facts.engines: Calls can use Jitsi or LiveKit; optional virtual-agent bots can connect to OpenAI or Azure OpenAI
facts.dataFormat: Hosted maps and account or room data live on WorkAdventure's EU service; self-hosted maps live on persistent volumes or S3-compatible storage, with original map sources kept separately by the user
facts.gapVsPaid: The ten-person cap, more technical map authoring and less polished video, admin and integrations are the clearest losses versus Gather.
facts.setupBlocker: Hosted use is clean; self-hosting needs Docker or Helm, domain/TLS, TURN and conferencing services, and serious map customization often starts in Tiled

rejectedAlternatives.name: Gather Trial
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Gather killed its permanent free tier; the current free story ends after thirty days.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Premium plan and a single private community DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Gather in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, WebSockets, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: host a small private spatial web room with basic movement and text presence, organize discussion into channels or topics, and keep membership and moderation under the owner's control.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement spaces, channels, topics, replies, reactions, mentions, profiles, roles, and invitations.
Use WebSockets for live updates but preserve every message transactionally in PostgreSQL.
Add moderation queues, reports, blocks, rate limits, attachment limits, and an audit log.
Provide email digests, browser notifications, search, pinned content, and member export.
Add owner-controlled retention, account deletion, backup, restore, and health checks.
Ship Docker Compose with a seeded demo, migrations, and an emergency admin command.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out public-network discovery and existing member liquidity.
Deliberately leave out production voice or video rooms.
Deliberately leave out native mobile applications, enterprise SSO, and 24-hour abuse operations.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
